title: The Jacobsthal function of the Gaussian integers
statement: For a bound X, let s(X) be the side of the largest square block of Gaussian integers {x + yi : x0 <= x < x0 + s, y0 <= y < y0 + s} in which every element is divisible by some Gaussian prime of norm at most X, that is, no element is coprime to the product of those primes. This is the two-dimensional analogue, for the Gaussian integers, of Jacobsthal's function j(m) at a primorial (the longest run of consecutive integers each sharing a factor with m). By the Chinese remainder theorem s(X) is also the largest s for which one residue class modulo each Gaussian prime of norm at most X covers an s x s square. The headline cell is X = 100, with the 25 Gaussian primes of norm at most 100 (up to units): find a square of side 16 or more in which every Gaussian integer has a prime factor of norm at most 100 (ours: side 15).
submission: Text file: one line 'x0 y0 s', the corner x0 + y0 i and the side s of the square (x0 and y0 may be large integers).
score: the side s of the square (larger is better)

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: weighted local search for one residue class per prime covering the 15 x 15 square (tools/src/gjacob.c, mode search), turned into a square of Gaussian integers by the Chinese remainder theorem (tools/gauss_jacobsthal.py); searches of 20 seconds with two seeds did not cover the 16 x 16 square

context: Jacobsthal's function j(m) is the smallest j such that every run of j consecutive integers contains one coprime to m. Its values at the primorials measure how long a run of integers can be sieved out by the small primes, which is the engine of every construction of long gaps between primes, from Westzynthius and Rankin to the work of Ford, Green, Konyagin, Maynard and Tao (2018), and it is computed exactly to large primorials (Hagedorn 2009; Ziller and Morack). Generalisations replace the run of integers by paired progressions (Ziller and Morack) or by the values of a polynomial (Kalmynin and Konyagin). In the Gaussian integers the natural run is a square block, and the same sieve gives squares of Gaussian integers with no prime among them far from the origin, the two-dimensional counterpart of long prime gaps (compare the Gaussian moat problem of Gethner, Wagon and Wick on walking through Gaussian primes). The sieve is richer than for the integers: a split prime p = 1 mod 4 contributes two prime ideals, each removing a different lattice line pattern of density 1/p, an inert prime q = 3 mod 4 removes only a sublattice of density 1/q^2, and 1 + i removes a checkerboard. The values below are exact up to X = 41 by an exhaustive search (the first uncovered point must be covered by some unused prime; branches are cut when the unused primes cannot cover what is left), and best known beyond.
references: E. Jacobsthal, Uber Sequenzen ganzer Zahlen, von denen keine zu n teilerfremd ist, I-III, Norske Vid. Selsk. Forh. (Trondheim) 33 (1960)
T. R. Hagedorn, Computation of Jacobsthal's function h(n) for n < 50, Math. Comp. 78 (2009) 1073-1087
M. Ziller, J. F. Morack, A short note on the computation of the generalised Jacobsthal function for paired progressions, arXiv:1706.03668
A. Kalmynin, S. Konyagin, A polynomial analogue of Jacobsthal function, arXiv:2302.00459
K. Ford, B. Green, S. Konyagin, J. Maynard, T. Tao, Long gaps between primes, J. Amer. Math. Soc. 31 (2018) 65-105
E. Gethner, S. Wagon, B. Wick, A stroll through the Gaussian primes, Amer. Math. Monthly 105 (1998) 327-337

novelty.verdict: new question for the Gaussian integers: Jacobsthal's function is studied for the integers and generalised to paired progressions and to polynomial values, but no Jacobsthal function of the Gaussian integers (or of another ring of integers) was found, as far as our searches show.
closest: Jacobsthal's function of the integers at primorials (Jacobsthal 1960; Hagedorn 2009; Ziller and Morack): runs of integers, not squares of Gaussian integers.

Generalised Jacobsthal functions for paired progressions (Ziller and Morack, arXiv:1706.03668) and for polynomial values (Kalmynin and Konyagin, arXiv:2302.00459): other generalisations, still over the integers.
The Gaussian moat problem (Gethner, Wagon and Wick 1998): gaps between Gaussian primes for a walk to infinity, a different question.
novelty.benchmark: no sieve or Jacobsthal family in the benchmark

columns: Gaussian primes of norm <= X (up to units)
rows: 9 by exhaustive search; 10 not decided in 900 s
first_values.note: Exact values: tools/src/gjacob.c, mode exact (s + 1 proved impossible: X = 37 in 4 s, X = 41 in 520 s); exhaustive searches over all residue classes for X = 5 and X = 13 in the tests agree. For X = 49 the exhaustive search covered the 9 x 9 square but did not settle 10 x 10 within 900 s. Best known values: mode search (weighted local search, 20 s for each attempt, two seeds); the gaps above them are open. The X = 100 square is in refs/gauss-jacobsthal.txt.
